quote: **OR 0.18** — family psychoeducation led 11 models for 12-month relapse prevention (Rodolico et al., *Lancet Psychiatry* 2022; 90 RCTs, >10,000 patients).
problem: My recollection of the Rodolico 2022 network meta-analysis is that the family-psychoeducation-vs-TAU estimate for 12-month relapse was nearer OR 0.33, and that the authors emphasized the intervention models did not clearly separate from one another; OR 0.18 may be a credible-interval bound or a transcription error, which would roughly double the taught effect. The figure is load-bearing: it recurs in this page's TL;DR ('OR 0.18, NNT 7 for relapse prevention'), in a key-points bullet, in the keyed quiz option and rationale, and on exp_family.md as 'Family psychoeducation lowers relapse from ~37% to ~10% (OR 0.18)' — the ~10% endpoint is back-derived from the same OR, so all instances stand or fall together. None of these carries an evidence annotation (the page's only registered evidence source is brown-1972-expressed-emotion), so the A4 gate cannot catch it. The keyed answer itself (family psychoeducation is the strongest-evidence choice) is correct regardless.
replacement: **OR ~0.33** — family psychoeducation ranked best of the family-intervention models for 12-month relapse prevention (Rodolico et al., *Lancet Psychiatry* 2022; 90 RCTs, >10,000 patients).
basis: Rodolico et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2022 — a single check of the paper's abstract/forest plot for the family-psychoeducation-vs-TAU 12-month relapse estimate settles this finding and the derived ~37%-to-~10% percentages on exp_family.md; I cannot specifically recall 0.18 as the point estimate.

verification.reasoning: Quote is verbatim (line 1069), but the claimed problem is not real: per the PubMed abstract of Rodolico et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2022;9(3):211-221 (PMID 35093198, doi:10.1016/S2215-0366(21)00437-5), the network meta-analysis compared 11 family intervention models across 90 RCTs with 10,340 participants, and 'ORs compared with treatment as usual ranged from 0·18 (95% CI 0·12-0·27) for family psychoeducation alone to 0·63 ... for community-based interventions', with the authors concluding family psychoeducation alone 'was superior to the more complex models.' OR 0.18 is therefore the point estimate, not a credible-interval bound or transcription error, and every element of the quoted sentence (0.18, led the 11 models, 90 RCTs, >10,000 patients) is faithful. The reviewer's OR ~0.33 recollection belongs to the companion NMA (Bighelli et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2021;8:969-980, doi:10.1016/S2215-0366(21)00243-1), whose differently-defined nodes gave family interventions OR 0.35, relapse-prevention programmes 0.33, and a family-psychoeducation node of 0.56 — a different analysis. Applying the proposed replacement would make the material wrong. The dependent instances (TL;DR, key point, quiz key, and exp_family's ~37%→~10%, which back-derives correctly from OR 0.18) all stand; the finding's own low confidence anticipated exactly this check, which resolves against it.

NNT 11 overstates naltrexone's effect relative to the very source the answer cites; the predecessor Jonas 2014 analysis reported NNT 12.

basis: McPheeters M et al., Pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis, JAMA 2023 (the cited key paper); verifying its NNT results settles it.

verification.reasoning: Quote is verbatim (V08 line 547) and the page's key paper is McPheeters et al., JAMA 2023 — but verification reverses the finding. Per that paper's PubMed abstract (doi:10.1001/jama.2023.19761): 'The numbers needed to treat to prevent 1 person from returning to any drinking were 11 (95% CI, 1-32) for acamprosate and 18 (95% CI, 4-32) for oral naltrexone at a dose of 50 mg/d. Compared with placebo, oral naltrexone (50 mg/d) was associated with lower rates of return to heavy drinking, with a number needed to treat of 11 (95% CI, 5-41).' The page's sentence — naltrexone NNT 11 for preventing return to heavy drinking; acamprosate NNT 11 for preventing any drinking — therefore matches its cited source exactly on both drugs and both outcomes. The reviewer transposed the outcomes: NNT 18 is oral naltrexone for return to ANY drinking, not heavy drinking. The proposed replacement ('naltrexone NNT = 18 for preventing return to heavy drinking') would insert a factual error into currently correct material. No real problem exists; rejected.

The suspicion of mis-extraction is disproven by the cited paper's own abstract: per PubMed, Rodolico et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2022 ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/S2215-0366(21)00437-5)) reports 'ORs compared with treatment as usual ranged from 0.18 (95% CI 0.12-0.27) for family psychoeducation alone to 0.63 (0.42-0.94) for community-based interventions,' with the conclusion that family psychoeducation alone was superior to more complex models — the page's OR, CI, comparator (TAU), timepoint (12-month primary), and 'most efficacious' framing all match the source exactly. quote: A network meta-analysis in 'Lancet Psychiatry' (2022) found that family psychoeducation in schizophrenia reduced 12-month relapse rates from 37% to what percentage?
problem: The keyed answer (10%) asserts a 73% relative reduction in 12-month relapse from an adjunctive psychosocial intervention — far beyond anything the family-intervention meta-analytic literature reports (roughly a halving of relapse, i.e. ~17-25% from a 37% baseline), and stronger than the effect of maintenance antipsychotics themselves. The 25% distractor is closer to the evidence, and its feedback ('This would be a significant reduction, but the actual data showed an even more robust effect') actively teaches the inflated figure. Likely a machine-extraction garble; the item should be re-keyed to 25% (or rewritten with the NMA's actual proportions) and both feedback strings fixed. Applies equally to residents.
replacement: Meta-analytic data, including the 2022 Lancet Psychiatry network meta-analysis of family interventions, show that family psychoeducation roughly halves 12-month relapse in schizophrenia. If relapse with usual care is 37%, approximately what relapse rate would be expected with family psychoeducation?
basis: Rodolico et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2022 (family interventions for relapse prevention in schizophrenia, NMA) and Bighelli et al., Lancet Psychiatry 2021 report roughly a halving of relapse odds vs usual care; Pitschel-Walz 2001 and the Cochrane review (Pharoah 2010) likewise show ~40-55% relative reduction, not 73%. Checking the relapse proportions in the 2022 NMA's results table would settle the exact keyed figure.

verification.reasoning: The quote is faithful, but the claimed problem is not real: the keyed 10% is consistent with the very NMA the stem cites. According to PubMed, the Rodolico et al. 2022 Lancet Psychiatry abstract (DOI https://doi.org/10.1016/S2215-0366(21)00437-5) reports that at the primary 12-month timepoint 'ORs compared with treatment as usual ranged from 0.18 (95% CI 0.12-0.27) for family psychoeducation alone to 0.63 (0.42-0.94) for community-based interventions', with family psychoeducation alone superior to the more complex models — and applying OR 0.18 to a 37% usual-care relapse rate yields ~9.6%, i.e., the keyed 10%. The reviewer's premise that the family-intervention literature reports 'roughly a halving' and that 10% is 'far beyond anything reported' is contradicted by the item's own cited source (the ~halving figures belong to the older meta-analyses the basis also cites, not to this NMA), and the reviewer's basis affirmatively mischaracterizes Rodolico 2022. Re-keying to 25% or rewriting to 'roughly halves', as the replacement proposes, would make the material contradict the paper it cites. Caveats — the abstract reports ORs rather than the raw 37%/10% proportions, and the authors grade confidence moderate to very low — could support a different, milder finding about presentation of derived figures, but not this finding's claim that the key is wrong.

quote: A 2025 RCT showed that DBT produced significantly fewer suicide-related events than SSRI and clinical management, emphasizing the role of psychotherapy.
problem: Cites an RCT I cannot identify in the literature through January 2026, and the same untraceable citation is echoed in Q2's feedback ('later research (2025) indicates DBT produces fewer suicide-related events than clinical management with SSRIs'). An effect claim hung on a design-plus-year with no study identity gives the learner nothing to trace and, if the NotebookLM extraction invented or garbled the reference, the deck teaches learners to cite a nonexistent trial. The underlying clinical point — psychotherapy, not SSRIs, is the primary treatment for suicide-related behavior in BPD — is correct and does not need this citation. Applies equally to residents.
replacement: Evidence-based psychotherapy is the primary treatment for reducing self-harm and suicide-related behavior in BPD; SSRIs have not been shown to prevent suicide-related events in BPD and are at most adjuncts for comorbid symptoms.
basis: No RCT randomizing patients with BPD to DBT versus SSRI-plus-clinical-management with a suicide-related-events outcome is identifiable as of January 2026 (Linehan 1991/2006 used TAU and community treatment by experts; McMain 2009 compared DBT with general psychiatric management). Locating the citation named in the source audio, or a PubMed search for it, would settle whether the trial exists; APA and NICE guidance for BPD support the corrected framing.

verification.reasoning: The quote is faithful, but the finding's core premise — that the 2025 RCT is untraceable and possibly nonexistent — is false. According to PubMed, the trial exists and matches the deck's description in design, year, comparator, population, and result: Brodsky BS, Galfalvy H, Mann JJ, Grunebaum MF, Stanley B, 'Dialectical Behavior Therapy Versus Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor Treatment for Suicidal Behavior in Borderline Personality Disorder: A Randomized Controlled Trial', Am J Psychiatry 2025;182(12):1083-1092 (DOI https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.20240298), which randomized 84 individuals with BPD to 6 months of DBT versus SSRIs with clinical management (SSRI/M) and found significantly fewer suicide-related events, fewer suicide attempts, and lower NSSI counts in the DBT arm during the treatment phase. The quoted feedback ('A 2025 RCT showed that DBT produced significantly fewer suicide-related events than SSRI and clinical management') is therefore an accurate one-line summary of a real, easily locatable trial — a targeted PubMed search on the deck's own descriptors surfaces it immediately — and the Q2 echo is likewise substantiated. The proposed replacement would strip a true, correctly characterized citation, so the finding fails on both the problem and the fix. (Optional polish, not an error: the deck could name the trial, and could note that 12-month follow-up outcomes were comparable between arms.)

quote: Mortality is roughly **six-fold higher in the four weeks after opioid agonist treatment stops** compared with time in treatment [9].
problem: This is the figure the page instructs the resident to say to the patient "plainly, as information", so its magnitude is load-bearing. My recollection of Santo et al. 2021 (ref [9]) and of the Sordo 2017 meta-analysis is that the excess in the four weeks after OAT cessation is on the order of two- to three-fold relative to time in treatment, not six-fold. The page's own Q6 restates the same reference as all-cause mortality "roughly half" during treatment versus out of it, which sits awkwardly beside a six-fold figure drawn from the same source. If six-fold is an overstatement, the error lands inside a counselling script.
replacement: Mortality is roughly **two- to three-fold higher in the four weeks after opioid agonist treatment stops** compared with time in treatment [9].
basis: Santo T et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2021 (ref [9]) reports pooled all-cause mortality rate ratios during OAT, out of OAT, and in the first four weeks after cessation; Sordo et al., BMJ 2017 reports approximately 32 versus 11 per 1000 person-years for methadone in the four weeks post-cessation versus in treatment. Reading the rate-ratio table in ref [9] for the "four weeks after cessation" stratum would settle this in one step.

quote: A real-world cohort showed **guideline-concordant first-line regimens cut 30-day rehospitalization (OR 0.21) and any readmission (OR 0.39)** vs. no treatment [4]
problem: The comparator is stated as 'no treatment,' which does not match what the cited study is asking. A paper titled 'Does the Ranking Matter?' is set up to contrast first-line against lower-ranked or non-recommended regimens, not treatment against nothing — and 'no treatment' is a near-empty comparator group in an acute-mania admission cohort. If the true reference group is non-first-line pharmacotherapy, these odds ratios are a genuinely strong argument for guideline concordance; if it really is untreated patients, they are close to uninformative and should not be handed to residents as 'a compelling lever for shared decision-making,' because the first patient who pushes back will find the confound immediately.
replacement: A real-world cohort showed **guideline-concordant first-line regimens cut 30-day rehospitalization (OR 0.21) and any readmission (OR 0.39)** compared with patients not discharged on a CANMAT first-line regimen [4]
basis: Gomes et al., 'Does the Ranking Matter?', Can J Psychiatry 2023;68(8):605–612 — this page's reference [4]. Settled by reading the study's stated reference group in its methods and confirming which contrast produced OR 0.21 and OR 0.39; the replacement text above assumes the first-line vs non-first-line contrast and should be adjusted if the paper genuinely used an untreated comparator.

verification.reasoning: The quote is verbatim (docs/curriculum-review/resident/02_CURRICULUM_V11.md, line 241; the finding's _source_path misstamps the ms3 file). The finding's central suspicion is settled against it by the paper itself. According to PubMed, the abstract of Gomes et al. 2023 (PMID 37551100, https://doi.org/10.1177/07067437231156235) classified discharge regimens as 'first-line, second-line, noncompliant, or no treatment' and reports exactly the quoted contrasts against no treatment: 'Compared to no treatment, only first-line treatments were associated with a statistically significant decreased risk of 30-day readmission (odds ratio [OR] = 0.209)' and 'the risk of any readmission was reduced by first-line (OR = 0.387) ... compared to no treatment.' The page's 'vs. no treatment [4]' is therefore a faithful summary of the study, and the proposed replacement ('compared with patients not discharged on a CANMAT first-line regimen') would make the material wrong — that contrast is not the one that produced OR 0.21/0.39. The reviewer's fallback ('should be adjusted if the paper genuinely used an untreated comparator') concedes this case, and the stated low confidence was warranted. The residual editorial point — that an untreated comparator is confounded, so 'a compelling lever for shared decision-making' oversells (the paper indeed also found noncompliant regimens reduced any-readmission, OR 0.414) — is a legitimate nuance but is not the claimed error, and the quoted sentence transparently names its comparator.
